hero.title: A good first house for your project
hero.subtitle: This is not a finished product. It is a simple, working website with pages, sign-in, and a few rules that keep your code — and your AI assistant — from getting messy. You do not need to understand everything today.

what.title: Not a finished app. A solid baseline.
what.body: Think of this as a furnished apartment. The kitchen is already in the same place every time. You can paint the walls, add rooms, or throw the furniture out later.

cards.title: A real website
cards.body: There are pages you can click. You can create an account and see a private dashboard. Nothing here is fake.

cards.title: Repeating recipes
cards.body: When we add a feature, we follow the same steps. That is what people mean by “patterns” — a recipe you reuse so you do not invent a new one every time.

cards.title: Easier for you and AI
cards.body: If the house is tidy, a coding assistant can find the kitchen. If every room is random, it guesses. Guesses go wrong.

start.title: Five small steps. Stop whenever you want.
start.subtitle: You do not need a job in software to do this. Read one step, do it, then come back.

steps.title: Look around
steps.body: You are already looking at the running site. Click around. You will not break the internet.

steps.title: Make a test account
steps.body: Use any email you own. While you work on your own computer, extra “verify your email” checks are usually turned off.

steps.title: Tell the AI what you are building
steps.body: Ask your AI to run the getting-started skill. It will ask a few questions (web or mobile, accounts, database) and write the answers into AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.

steps.title: Ask for one tiny change
steps.body: Try: “Add a page at /hello that says hello.” Watch which files change. That is the pattern you will reuse.

steps.title: Add a database when you need one
steps.body: Copy .env.example to .env.local. For a free database on your machine, run docker compose up from the project root. You can do this later.

patterns.title: Four habits that keep the project calm
patterns.subtitle: You do not have to memorize these. Just know they exist, so you or your AI can copy them.

items.title: The kitchen and the pantry
items.body: A Service decides what is allowed. A Repository talks to the database. Keep those jobs separate and every change stays smaller.

items.title: One front door
items.body: API routes go through the route wrapper. That helper checks who you are before the rest of the code runs.

items.title: Pages ask the server. The server asks a service.
items.body: Code in the browser never talks to the database. Page handlers and the JSON API call the same services on the server, so the rules live in one place.

items.title: Check the form before you trust it
items.body: Validators describe what valid data looks like, with plain names like UpdateUserSettings. Every entry point uses the same ones, so fewer surprises.

later.title: Things you can ignore until you need them

items.title: A database on the internet
items.body: Neon or Supabase will host Postgres for you. For learning, Docker on your machine is enough.

items.title: Real emails
items.body: Resend can send password-reset and “verify your email” messages. Skip this while you learn.

items.title: Putting it on the internet
items.body: Railway is a friendly host for this stack: one small binary. Any host that runs a container works too. Wait until the app does something you want to show people.

remove.title: This welcome page is designed to be thrown away
remove.body: None of your real app lives in this folder. Login, signup, and the dashboard stay.
steps: Open the routes config in apps/web/internal/config and set TemplateWelcome to false.
Remove the welcome routes where apps/web/ui mounts them (the compiler shows you where).
remove.note: That is the whole cleanup. Read the README inside apps/web/ui/welcome if you want it written down.

why.eyebrow: Why the house is built this way
why.title: Same steps, every time
why.subtitle: Beginners and AI assistants both do better when the next file has an obvious place to go. That is all “architecture” means here.
why.introTitle: A messy house is hard for everyone
why.introBody: If login code lives in five different styles, you have to re-learn the project every day. Your AI has to guess. Guessing is how bugs show up. These four recipes are the opposite of guessing.

items.title: Service / repository
items.analogy: The kitchen decides the meal. The pantry only stores food. If the pantry starts deciding meals, you can never find anything.
items.lookHere: Look here when you add a rule like “only you can edit your name”.

items.title: One API wrapper
items.analogy: Every guest uses the same front door. The door checks ID. Nobody climbs through a window.
items.lookHere: Wrap every new /api route with it.

items.title: Handlers call services
items.analogy: The customer asks a waiter. The waiter walks into the kitchen. Customers do not wander into the fridge.
items.lookHere: Page handlers call services in-process. Browser code never reaches the database.

items.title: Validators
items.analogy: A bouncer with a list. If the name is missing, the person does not get in. The list is also the Go type.
items.lookHere: Put new form rules in the validate package, named after what they check.
